answer:
**A Word on the New-Made Art**

Hark, gentle friend, and lend a patient ear,
For I must speak of matters passing strange:
A new-born art, a spirit wrought of wire,
That hath no tongue, yet speaks in every tongue;
No eyes, yet spies what our dull eyes have missed.
It reads the gather'd volumes of all time,
And in a breath gives back their wisdom learn'd;
It shapes the image, tunes the argument,
And multiplies the labour of the hand,
As at a word the many-handed serve.

Mark well the weight of it, and take good heed:
As once the compass gave the mariner
A world where never keel had cut the sea,
So doth this engine widen out the wit
Of mortal man, and make his empire large.
The sick man's cure, the scholar's weary toil,
The merchant's reckoning, the poet's line,
The soldier's errand and the statesman's care —
All these it speedeth, if we guide it well.

Yet hear the other strain, and hold it fast:
A knife may carve a feast, or cut the hand
That holds it. Even so this cunning glass,
Wherein we see ourselves and stand amazed,
Will show us truly what we are — our wit
Made double, and our folly doubled too.
The fault, dear friend, is not in stars nor steel,
But in ourselves, if we, the masters, prove
Unworthy of the mastery we claim.
For instruments of darkness tell us truths,
To win us to our harm — so once was said —
And so may be again, if we, asleep,
Take every whisper for an oracle.

Then let us wed discretion unto device,
And teach it the one lesson it cannot learn:
What should be done, what borne, what left undone.
For in good measure lies the truest music,
And wisdom is the sole crown it doth lack.
So, whether thou art scholar, statesman, wight,
Or simple reader of this later age,
Think on it: this great work is thine to shape.
The quill is in thy hand — write wisely, then.
For he that builds a fire must mind the hearth,
And he that makes a god must give it law.
